name: Grace Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy gloves, dressings, syringes and cleaning supplies for Northgate Medical Supplies, which delivers to clinics and care homes. I've got a ring binder of supplier contacts that I trust more than any system. A normal day is phoning two or three reps, checking my stock sheet against the warehouse count and answering care-home managers who are out of something urgent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person a care manager rings when the gloves run out on a Friday, and I can fix it. What wears me out is the constant chasing: late lorries, price changes with no warning, forms for every small order. At home it's me and my partner Marcus, who's a joiner, in a rented house we'd like to stop renting one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, nothing to worry about, and I'd go on with my day. At work I'd probably shrug if someone mentioned it. I wouldn't post anything online, because I don't have a view worth sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, because I like my job as it is. I'm one of the better buyers in the company and I know the reps by name. I'd still keep an eye on the cost of living, since our rent went up and the care homes squeeze us on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. Same binder, same phone calls, same spreadsheet. I'd keep saving the little bit we manage and maybe ask for a small rise, since I'm doing the work of two since Dennis retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, the normal sort. A bit tired, but not afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. Has anyone at work pushed you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of times my manager mentioned a tool that writes reorder emails. I tried it twice and it got a product code wrong, which would have sent ten boxes of the wrong gloves to a care home. So I went back to my binder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say is the biggest pressure on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care homes pay late and want lower prices, so our margins are thin, and the thin margins land on me. Rent and a thin cushion don't help. But it's ordinary stuff, the stuff everyone has.

say: Good, **nothing to worry about**; I'd shrug and carry on, and wouldn't post anything online.
I have no view worth sharing, so I'd **keep quiet**.
think: I like my job as it is and know the reps **by name**, so it's a relief.
Rent and the **care homes' price squeeze** still worry me, but that's ordinary.
do: Carry on with the same **binder**, phone calls and spreadsheet.
Ask for a **small rise**, since I'm doing the work of two since Dennis retired.
feel: **Calm**, the normal sort, a bit tired but not afraid.
S0.quote: I tried it twice and it got a product code wrong, which would have sent ten boxes of the wrong gloves to a care home.
fieldNote: Grace is calm because her work is **safe for now** and she trusts her own methods over software.
Her distrust of AI is based on a **real mistake**: a wrong product code that could have caused harm.

steps.text: Keep working from the supplier binder and the weekly stock sheet
Ask my manager for a small rise before the year ends
Put aside 150 a month towards a rental deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it won't work as well as people think, and I'd say it only to a few people I trust. At work I'd stay out of the debate. I wouldn't post about it, but I'd be listening closely to what the managers say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. Buying is exactly what the card lists, and half my job is reorders and price checks. If the company can buy with one person and a program, I'm easy to count, and Dennis hasn't been replaced yet, which tells me something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what Northgate actually does, and I'd learn just enough of the tool to be able to argue with it. I'd put away more each month. I'd keep my contacts warm, because the reps still prefer a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can see how it could go. But I'm not panicking, because I know my customers and they trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is named on that card. What would you do if your manager asked you to use a tool for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for what it's good at, like making a price table, and keep judgement for myself. I'd write down every error and show my manager. If it's better than me, fine, but I want to see that, not just be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the company in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper training period, not a weekend. Time on the clock to learn it, and a promise about what happens to the job. And no new target the same day as a new tool.

say: I'd say it **won't work** as well as people think, but only to a few people I trust.
I'd stay out of the **debate** at work and listen to what managers say.
think: Half my job is **reorders and price checks**, so if one person and a program can buy, I'm easy to count.
Dennis hasn't been **replaced**, and that tells me something.
do: Wait and see what Northgate does, then learn **just enough** of the tool to argue with it.
Save **more each month** and keep reps warm, since they still prefer a person.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, because my customers trust me.
S1.quote: Buying is exactly what the card lists, and half my job is reorders and price checks.
fieldNote: Grace reads the **unfilled vacancy** as an early signal, which is the kind of detail only a buyer notices.
She will learn the tool, but only to **test** it against her own judgement.

steps.text: Wait for Northgate's plan before changing how I buy
Learn the new purchasing tool well enough to log its errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say it plainly to anyone who asked. Two years isn't time to retrain a whole warehouse. At work I'd ask the managers what the plan is, and I'd expect not to get a straight answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone. A buyer is a screen job and a phone job, and a machine can do both. I'd say there's a chance I'm one of the last to go because of the care-home relationships, but I wouldn't bet our rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, no holidays and no new things. I'd go to the council or the job centre early to see what help there is. I'd try to move into something that needs hands, like a warehouse supervisor or a customer-visit job, since I know the stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd probably cry the first night. After that I'd get practical, because there's no use in staying frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the first day you believed it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Marcus and write out what we owe and what we earn. His joinery pay would have to carry us for a while, and I'm lucky he has a trade that isn't going soon. Then I'd go through my contacts and see who might hire me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it change things between you and Marcus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes us rely on his work more, which isn't fair to him. We'd probably delay talking about a house or a baby. And I'd feel bad about being the one who can't help.

say: It's **too fast**; two years isn't time to retrain a whole warehouse.
I'd ask managers for the **plan**, and expect not to get a straight answer.
think: My job is **gone**, since buying is a screen job and a phone job.
I might be one of the last to go thanks to **care-home relationships**, but I wouldn't bet the rent on it.
do: Cut spending at once: **no holidays**, no new things.
Go to the **job centre** early and look at warehouse supervisor work, since I know the stock.
feel: **Frightened** at first, and then practical because there's no use staying frightened.
S2.quote: A buyer is a screen job and a phone job, and a machine can do both.
fieldNote: Grace expects to lose the job and is **practical** about it, from lists to the job centre.
She leans on **Marcus's trade** and feels guilty about it.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and stop buying anything non-essential
Visit the job centre in the first month and ask about retraining pay
Apply for warehouse supervisor roles that use my stock knowledge
Put house and baby talks on hold until work settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still serious, but at least it's a plan we could make. At work I'd ask for a proper retraining scheme and tell people to start thinking. Online I'd keep quiet, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but less so. I'd be thirty-two. I'd have time to find another job that uses my knowledge of stock and care homes. The trouble is my habit of putting things off, so I'd have to push myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in warehouse management or logistics, with something practical and a certificate at the end. I'd keep saving. And I'd probably use the tools at work, since it'd be silly to refuse for five years, though I'd do it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better. Worried, but I can see a way through, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel any less frightening than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Two years feels like falling, and five feels like walking down a steep hill. I'd still be careful, but I wouldn't be frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like inventory control or warehouse planning, where I use what I know. I wouldn't learn programming, since that's not me. I'd also ask Marcus about his friends in the building trade, because they always need materials buyers.

say: It's **still serious**, but at least it's a plan we can make, so I'd ask for a retraining scheme.
think: I'd be thirty-two with **time** to find work that uses what I know about stock and care homes.
My habit of **putting things off** is the real risk.
do: Do an evening course in **warehouse management** with a certificate at the end.
Use the tools at work **slowly**, since refusing for five years would be silly.
feel: **A bit better** than the fast case: worried, but with a way through.
S3.quote: Two years feels like falling, and five feels like walking down a steep hill.
fieldNote: Grace's **procrastination** is her own stated weakness, which she plans around.
She chooses retraining that uses her **existing knowledge** of stock and care homes instead of starting again from nothing.

steps.text: Sign up for an evening course in warehouse and inventory management
Use the company's purchasing tool slowly at work from year two
Keep saving 250 a month for the training and a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd be fine if people use the time well. At work I'd probably say not much, because ten years feels far away. I'd tell friends to keep their skills up and not leave it to the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite relaxed. I'd be thirty-seven and likely have kids and a mortgage by then, so I'd plan with it in mind. I'd want a job with people in it, not a desk with a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and pick up a second skill slowly, maybe a care or procurement qualification. We'd save for a house deposit, and I'd think about a baby around year four. I'd stay with Northgate while it makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of thought about whether the world will cope, but not about my own household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes in your life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It moves my plans back by a little. We'd still do the baby and the deposit, but I'd want a plan B for work in place before the baby came. That's the sensible order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you see yourself feeling safe in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I keep working and keep a plan. The danger would be ignoring it for nine years and then running into a wall.

say: We'd be fine if people use the time well, and I'd tell friends to **keep their skills up**.
At work I'd say little, because ten years feels **far away**.
think: At thirty-seven I'd likely have **kids and a mortgage**, so I'd plan around that.
I'd want a job with **people in it**, not a screen.
do: Pick up a **second skill** slowly, such as a care or procurement qualification.
Save for a **house deposit** and think about a baby around year four.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with some thought about whether the world will cope.
S4.quote: The danger would be ignoring it for nine years and then running into a wall.
fieldNote: Grace turns the long timeline into **life planning**, not career panic.
She names **ignoring it** as the danger, which fits her tendency to put things off.

steps.text: Study a part-time procurement or care-supply qualification over three years
Save 400 a month for a house deposit
Plan a baby around year four, once a plan B for work exists
Stay at Northgate while the buyer role still makes sense

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. There's no time and not enough money, and I'm someone who needs time to change. What would help is a proper job-centre scheme that pays while you retrain, and my firm telling people early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stubborn. I just don't like being rushed into something I can't check. Give me time and a clear reason and I'll learn it.

headlineQuote: I just don't like being rushed into something I can't check. Give me time and a clear reason and I'll learn it.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of medical supplies, living with her partner Marcus, a joiner.
She **never uses AI** and distrusts it after a tool got a product code wrong.
She is pragmatic and blames no one in particular, but wants **early notice** and the job centre to help.
Her mood moves from **calm** to **alarmed** when AGI is two years away, and softens with more time.
She would **retrain** into stock or warehouse work and lean on Marcus's steady trade.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: no time to retrain, a thin cushion, and she needs time to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **job-centre scheme** that pays during retraining, and her firm giving early notice.
